summary: Canadian Coast Guard light on a rocky islet where Fitzhugh Sound meets Lama Passage: lit 1899, de-staffed 1989, reached only by boat.

lens.note: Apparatus as described in the 1899 notice (quoted by LighthouseFriends). The sources read do not describe the present apparatus.

structures.note: Per the Department's 1899 notice as LighthouseFriends prints it: 30 ft high, red roof, red lantern. Replaced later.
Erected three years after a second dwelling was built in 1964, when the 1949 concrete building was replaced (LighthouseFriends).
8 m (26 ft) round cylindrical white tower per Rowlett, dated 1989. LighthouseFriends describes a cylindrical column erected after the buildings were demolished.

access.note: Reached only by boat. Grounds open; tower closed (Rowlett; LighthouseFriends).

events.note: Square white wooden building with red roof and red lantern, 30 ft (9.1 m) high, built by departmental labour under foreman D. M. Fraser (the notice as LighthouseFriends prints it).
Put in operation 15 November 1899. Fixed white light, 42 ft (12.8 m) above high water, visible 12 miles (the notice as LighthouseFriends prints it).
James Codville appointed 26 December 1899 (1910 keepers' table, page image checked). The 1913 table gives 24 October 1900 for the same station (page image checked).
Benjamin Codville took charge on his father's death (LighthouseFriends).

The Department decided in 1949, after the Egg Island light was destroyed in November 1948, to build a similar concrete combined tower and dwelling with a fog-alarm building. The completion year is not given.
From fixed white to four seconds on, four seconds off (LighthouseFriends).
Diaphone fog alarm, a three-second blast every twenty seconds in thick weather. The keepers' hand horn ended (LighthouseFriends).
A separate dwelling built to house a second keeper (LighthouseFriends).
Concrete building replaced by a new dwelling and a skeletal tower (LighthouseFriends).
De-staffed in March 1989 (LighthouseFriends). The light stayed active.
Present round white cylindrical tower, 8 m (26 ft), dated 1989 by Rowlett.

corrections.why: The standing tower is the round white cylinder dated 1989 (Rowlett; LighthouseFriends describes it after the 1989 demolition). The 1899 tower was a 30 ft wooden building, since replaced.
The light was not deactivated. LighthouseFriends records de-staffing in March 1989, Rowlett lists it as Active, and the Coast Guard's list gives its present characteristic.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The record's conflict between first year and present tower is resolved: the first light (wooden, lit 15 November 1899) and the present cylindrical tower (dated 1989) are different structures, so 1899 stands as the first-lit year.

LighthouseFriends gives the 1949 pattern as four seconds on and four off. Rowlett's present pattern (4 s on, 2 s off) agrees with the Coast Guard's Oc W 6s. The record's Oc W 6s stands; the date of the change is not given in the sources read.
The 1899 notice gives 'visible 12 miles' without naming the unit. The Coast Guard's present nominal range is 8 nautical miles, which the record keeps.

notes_for_editor: Both keepers' tables were checked against the page images. 1910 table (scan p.179, printed p.172): the Pointer Island row reads 'Jas. Codville, Dec. 26, 1899, 465 00' with the columns aligned. 1913 table (scan p.81, printed p.74): '*Pointer island, J. Codville, Oct. 24, 1900, 570 00'; the date and salary are visible on the image only, not in the OCR. The two tables disagree and the story states both. The 1900 Marine report's new-lights list does not name Pointer Island in its OCR, so the 15 November 1899 date rests on LighthouseFriends' transcription of the Department's notice; a primary copy was not located. The keeper names after 1946 are from LighthouseFriends alone (the corpus holds no Marine reports after 1924); they are facts from a community site. The Walbran account is quoted from LighthouseFriends; the original was not located. The keepers from about 1960 on (Bigelow, Carson, Toner) are named only, in their public role, with no personal detail. No storm, wreck or rescue tied to this station appears in the sources read; the 1948 loss was the Egg Island light. Rowlett spells the sound 'Fitz Hugh'; the story keeps LighthouseFriends' 'Fitzhugh'. The 1900 report spells the captain 'Wallbran'. Coast Guard list entry 592 checked (12.9 m, 8 NM, Oc W 6s). Record errors: the 1899 tower is not the standing tower, and the 1989 event is de-staffing, not deactivation.
